Fundus and angiographic findings show optic disc leakage (papillitis) and peripapillary hemorrhages plus fluorescein leakage from retinal venules (retinal vasculitis). Concomitant mild anterior chamber and vitreous inflammation point to an inflammatory/post‑infectious or immune‑mediated process involving both the optic nerve head and the retina. Timing (day 2 of hospitalization) and a positive nasopharyngeal SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR strongly suggest a para‑infectious or direct SARS‑CoV‑2–associated inflammatory optic neuropathy/retinal vasculitis; CSF SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR was negative (common in para‑infectious immune reactions). MRI can be normal early in optic neuritis, so normal MRI does not exclude optic neuritis. The pattern of severe vision loss, disc swelling with peripapillary hemorrhages and intraocular inflammation is also characteristic of MOG‑IgG–associated optic neuritis (MOGAD). AQP4‑IgG NMOSD is another immune cause of severe optic neuritis in middle‑aged women. Herpesvirus posterior uveitis/acute retinal necrosis can produce retinal vasculitis and optic nerve involvement but serologies and clinical pattern make it less likely here. Ischemic optic neuropathy (arteritic or non‑arteritic) is less consistent because of pain on eye movement, inflammatory signs and retinal venous leakage, but remains a differential given age. Therefore the ranked differential emphasizes SARS‑CoV‑2–associated para‑infectious optic neuritis with retinal vasculitis first, then immune antibody‑mediated optic neuritis (MOG, AQP4), then viral posterior uveitis, then ischemic optic neuropathy.

DIAGNOSIS:
1) SARS‑CoV‑2–associated (para‑infectious/post‑infectious) optic neuritis with retinal vasculitis (optic papillitis)  
2) MOG‑IgG–associated optic neuritis (MOG antibody disease) with concomitant retinal vasculitis  
3) AQP4‑IgG–positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (severe optic neuritis)  
4) Herpesvirus (VZV/HSV) posterior uveitis/acute retinal necrosis with optic nerve involvement  
5) Ischemic optic neuropathy (arteritic or non‑arteritic AION)

Case Information:
A woman in her late 50s was hospitalized in March 2020 for severe bilateral pneumonia. She had recent close contact with a fatal case. No relevant medical history was reported. On day 2 post-admission, she developed blurred vision and redness in her right eye and temporary (8-day) pain when mobilizing the globe.

Physical Examination:
Best-corrected visual acuity was +2 logMAR (hand movement) OD and 0 logMAR OS. The right eye had:- Relative afferent pupil defect- Central scotoma- Impaired color and contrast vision- Central nongranulomatous retrodescemetic precipitates - Mild anterior chamber inflammation- Noticeable pupillary edema- 2 peripapillary hemorrhages- Mild vitreous inflammation- Retinal vessel narrowing in the inferior retinaContralateral eye examinations were normal. No other neurological symptoms were observed.

Diagnostic Tests:
